thread.title: For Microsoft The Future Is Now - Microsoft Corporation (NASDAQ:MSFT)

author: Michael Henage
title: For Microsoft The Future Is Now - Microsoft Corporation (NASDAQ:MSFT)
text:
The lost decade… three years ago, Microsoft (NASDAQ: MSFT ) was blasted by critics as dead money. The stock had a nice yield, but could the company grow again? When a stock stays in a tight trading range of about $28 to $33, investors and analysts have every right to be skeptical. In August 2015, I wrote an article on this very site making a few bold predictions about Microsoft in 2018 . One reader suggested I follow up to see how these predictions played out and that’s exactly what I’d like to do.
The Surface Phone? In 2015, Microsoft had just written down a portion of its Nokia (NYSE: NOK ) investment. Satya Nadella said the company would “generate new growth… on our own differentiated first-party premium device portfolio.” My first prediction was that Microsoft would release its own smartphone and that, in conjunction, the company would make it easy to port Alphabet (NASDAQ: GOOGL ) (NASDAQ: GOOG ) Android apps to the Windows app store. With these expectations, it seemed likely that Windows apps would expand to over 750,000 by 2018 and that Microsoft would take as much as 8% of mobile market share.
Three years ago, many analysts believed that Microsoft had to gain market share in mobile in order to regain relevance. Let’s just say that both the analysts and myself were very wrong. Not only did Microsoft not release its own smartphone, but the company appears to have given up on the smartphone hardware business. As of May 2018, Windows holds less than 1% market share . While the Windows Apps store has grown to about 669,000 apps , these are aimed at making the company’s tablet and touchscreen laptops more useful.
Though this data could be interpreted as negative for Microsoft, the company made a very sound business decision. Android holds a commanding 76% of smartphone market share, and Apple’s (NASDAQ: AAPL ) iOS carries nearly 19%. Microsoft’s choice was to focus on apps for Android and iOS instead of trying to wrestle market share from two very entrenched ecosystems. Whether you have an iPhone, Samsung, Google Pixel, or almost any other smartphone, there are numerous Microsoft apps to help you be more productive.
The more things change, the more they stay the same Whether it’s 2000, 2015, or 2018, one thing Microsoft investors count on is the dominance of Office. In my prior article, I suggested that Apple might shutter its productivity suite as it doesn’t fit with the company’s overall portfolio. As of last quarter, more than 78% of Apple’s revenue was from hardware. Though the company’s services and other products are growing fast, no one is suggesting that Pages, Numbers, and Keynote are the future of the company.
Most of Alphabet’s 23% adjusted revenue growth last quarter came from advertising. The company offers Google Docs for free, but these services seem to draw users to the company’s other properties. In 2015 and today, it seems Google could decide to change Google Docs to a subscription service if it felt users wouldn’t revolt. In either case Google Docs isn’t a make-or-break service for Alphabet.
On the other hand, Office hasn’t needed its competitors to drop away in order for it to continue its impressive growth. Microsoft’s Productivity and Business Processes made up over 33% of revenue and grew 14% in constant currency. The move to Office 365 has been seamless, and as I predicted in 2015, Skype and Cortana have been integrated so users can take advantage of these in conjunction with Office.
A Cloudy Past, Present, and Future In 2015, Microsoft generated $8 billion in cloud revenue. My prediction was the company would generate $20 billion in commercial cloud revenue by 2018. It seems this prediction was a little too aggressive, but not by much.
Microsoft’s current quarter shows $9 billion in revenue from Productivity and Business Processes leveraging cloud-based offerings. The company now generates almost 30% of its revenue from a division called Intelligent Cloud, which makes up almost $8 billion. Though it’s hard to tell how much of this revenue is cloud-based versus traditional software, almost $17 billion in revenue tied to the cloud is a significant jump from three years ago.
Given the popularity of Office 365, LinkedIn, and cloud services offered to businesses, it’s likely that Microsoft’s future is tied to the cloud as much now as it was three years ago.
What’s next? One of the predictions I’m most proud of from my prior article is the earnings, P/E, and stock price assumptions. I suggested investors would realize that Microsoft was once again a growth story and the stock would reach a forward P/E of 20. I expected earnings per share of $4 in 2018, implying a stock price of $80.
What happened is, next year’s average predicted EPS for Microsoft is $4.01. The stock trades right around $100, with a forward P/E of about 25. Investors who listened in 2015 benefited from over 44% compound annual growth, excluding dividends, over the last 3 years.
Now that we know where Microsoft has been, where does it go from here? In short, I believe analysts are underestimating the company’s growth, but investors are living a little too much in the past.
The average analyst expects the company to only grow earnings by over 4% next year. However, in the last 90 days, estimates for current year earnings have increased by 5%. Over the last four quarters, Microsoft has made analysts look silly, blasting past estimates by an average of 22%. This streak seems poised to continue as companies big and small look for solutions to their software and cloud service needs.
Even with this positive news on the earnings front, Microsoft’s stock isn’t the value that it once was. In 2015, the yield was north of 3%, today that yield is closer to 1.6%. Three years ago, the company’s forward P/E ratio was in the teens; today that number sits north of 25. Microsoft has proven it is still a growth story, but investors who are up significantly over the last few years should temper their expectations. Waiting for a pullback to pick up shares below $80 would be a better entry point for new money.
Disclosure: I am/we are long AAPL, MSFT.
